---
title: "hb_area() Engines: INLA vs JAX on CPU and Apple GPU (Metal)"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.2, dpi = 110)
library(ggplot2)

bench_file <- Filter(file.exists, c(
  file.path("..", "..", "inst", "extdata", "hb_engine_benchmark.rds"),
  file.path("inst", "extdata", "hb_engine_benchmark.rds")
))[1]
bench <- readRDS(bench_file)
tm <- bench$timings
ag <- bench$agreement
meta <- bench$meta

engine_labels <- c(inla = "INLA (inla_engine)",
                   cpu = "JAX NUTS, CPU (jax_engine(device = \"cpu\"))",
                   metal = "JAX NUTS, Apple GPU (jax_engine(device = \"metal\"))")
engine_colours <- c(inla = "#1D6A5C", cpu = "#E69F00", metal = "#7B5EA7")
design_labels <- c(gaussian = "Fay-Herriot (Gaussian)", beta = "Beta (proportions)")
short_labels <- c(gaussian = "Gaussian", beta = "Beta")
tm$engine_f <- factor(tm$engine, levels = names(engine_labels))
tm$design_f <- factor(design_labels[tm$design], levels = design_labels)
fmt_s <- function(x) ifelse(x < 10, sprintf("%.1f s", x), sprintf("%s s", format(round(x), big.mark = ",")))
n_max <- max(tm$n)
at_max <- function(design, engine, col = "time_warm") {
  tm[tm$design == design & tm$engine == engine & tm$n == n_max, col]
}
```

`hb_area()` can be estimated by two engines:

- **`inla_engine()`** (default): integrated nested Laplace approximation with
  [INLA](https://www.r-inla.org).
- **`jax_engine()`**: full MCMC with NumPyro's No-U-Turn sampler on
  [JAX](https://jax.readthedocs.io). It runs on the CPU, on an NVIDIA GPU
  (`device = "cuda"`) or on the GPU of Apple silicon (`device = "metal"`).

This page compares the speed of the engines and how closely their estimates
agree, on one Apple silicon machine.

## Setup

```{r setup-table}
py <- meta$python
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Item = c("Machine", "R", "fastsae", "INLA", "JAX / jax-metal / NumPyro", "MCMC settings",
           "Data", "Timing"),
  Value = c(meta$machine, meta$r_version, meta$fastsae, meta$inla,
            if (is.null(py)) "-" else paste(py[["jax"]], "/", py[["jax-metal"]], "/", py[["numpyro"]]),
            meta$jax_settings,
            "`sim_area_data(D = n, n_unsampled = 0, seed = 42 + n)`; `y ~ x1 + x2`",
            sprintf("Each fit run %d times on the same data; the first run includes JAX compilation", meta$reps))
))
```

Each engine runs in a separate R process, because JAX fixes its device at
the first fit of a session. The code is in
[`benchmarks/bench_hb_area_engines.R`](https://github.com/ridsonap/fastsae/blob/main/benchmarks/bench_hb_area_engines.R).

## Computation time

```{r time-plot, fig.cap = "Warm computation time (log scales). Lower is faster."}
ggplot(tm, aes(n, time_warm, colour = engine_f)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  facet_wrap(~design_f) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = function(x) paste(format(x, scientific = FALSE, drop0trailing = TRUE), "s")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = engine_colours, labels = engine_labels, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Number of domains (D)", y = "Time (seconds)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.direction = "vertical",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.spacing = grid::unit(1.5, "lines"))
```

```{r time-table}
wide <- reshape(tm[, c("design", "n", "engine", "time_warm")], idvar = c("design", "n"),
                timevar = "engine", direction = "wide")
names(wide) <- sub("^time_warm\\.", "", names(wide))
first <- reshape(tm[, c("design", "n", "engine", "time_first")], idvar = c("design", "n"),
                 timevar = "engine", direction = "wide")
names(first) <- sub("^time_first\\.", "", names(first))
tab <- data.frame(
  Model = design_labels[wide$design],
  D = format(wide$n, big.mark = ","),
  INLA = fmt_s(wide$inla),
  `JAX CPU` = fmt_s(wide$cpu),
  `JAX Metal` = fmt_s(wide$metal),
  `JAX Metal, first run` = fmt_s(first$metal),
  `Metal vs CPU` = ifelse(wide$metal > wide$cpu,
                          sprintf("%.1fx slower", wide$metal / wide$cpu),
                          sprintf("**%.1fx faster**", wide$cpu / wide$metal)),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(tab[order(tab$Model, wide$n), ], row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrrr")
```

```{r crossover}
speedup <- merge(tm[tm$engine == "metal", c("design", "n", "time_warm")],
                 tm[tm$engine == "cpu", c("design", "n", "time_warm")],
                 by = c("design", "n"), suffixes = c("_metal", "_cpu"))
speedup$metal_faster <- speedup$time_warm_metal < speedup$time_warm_cpu
first_metal <- function(design) {
  s <- speedup[speedup$design == design & speedup$metal_faster, ]
  if (nrow(s) == 0) NA else min(s$n)
}
cross <- vapply(names(design_labels), first_metal, numeric(1))
cross_txt <- vapply(names(design_labels), function(d) {
  if (is.na(cross[[d]])) {
    sprintf("for the %s model the CPU is faster at every $D$ tested", short_labels[[d]])
  } else {
    sprintf("for the %s model Metal is faster at $D = %s$ and above", short_labels[[d]],
            format(cross[[d]], big.mark = ","))
  }
}, character(1))
metal_growth <- function(design) {
  m <- tm[tm$design == design & tm$engine == "metal", ]
  m$time_warm[m$n == max(m$n)] / m$time_warm[m$n == min(m$n)]
}
cpu_growth <- function(design) {
  m <- tm[tm$design == design & tm$engine == "cpu", ]
  m$time_warm[m$n == max(m$n)] / m$time_warm[m$n == min(m$n)]
}
```

The results:

- **INLA is the fastest engine at every size.** It does not sample, so its
  time grows slowly with $D$. For example, the Gaussian model at
  $D = `r format(n_max, big.mark = ",")`$ takes `r fmt_s(at_max("gaussian", "inla"))`.
- **Metal has a large fixed cost per fit but grows slowly with $D$.** NUTS
  builds each trajectory in a loop whose length depends on the data, and on
  Metal every pass through that loop waits for the GPU and the CPU to
  synchronise. For the Gaussian model, going from
  $D = `r format(min(tm$n), big.mark = ",")`$ to
  $D = `r format(n_max, big.mark = ",")`$ multiplies the Metal time by
  `r sprintf("%.1f", metal_growth("gaussian"))` and the CPU time by
  `r sprintf("%.0f", cpu_growth("gaussian"))`.
- **CPU or GPU?** The CPU is faster for small and medium numbers of domains.
  The GPU catches up as $D$ grows: `r paste(cross_txt, collapse = ", and ")`
  (of the sizes tested).
  `jax_engine(device = "auto")` therefore keeps the CPU on macOS, and
  `device = "metal"` pays off only for large models.

## Agreement of the estimates

The JAX fits are compared with INLA on the same data. `cor` is the
correlation of the posterior means, `max |diff|` is the largest absolute
difference between them, and `sd ratio` is the median ratio of the
posterior standard deviations (JAX / INLA).

```{r agreement}
ag_tab <- data.frame(
  Model = design_labels[ag$design],
  Engine = c(cpu = "JAX CPU", metal = "JAX Metal")[ag$engine],
  D = format(ag$n, big.mark = ","),
  cor = sprintf("%.5f", ag$cor_hb),
  `max |diff|` = signif(ag$max_abs_diff_hb, 2),
  `sd ratio` = sprintf("%.3f", ag$median_ratio_sd),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(ag_tab[order(ag_tab$Model, ag_tab$Engine, ag$n), ], row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r rhat}
rh <- tm[tm$engine != "inla", ]
```

```{r sd-range}
sd_range <- function(design) {
  r <- range(ag$median_ratio_sd[ag$design == design])
  sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", r[1], r[2])
}
```

The posterior means of both MCMC engines agree with INLA, with correlations of
at least `r sprintf("%.4f", floor(min(ag$cor_hb) * 1e4) / 1e4)`. The posterior
standard deviations agree closely for the Gaussian model (ratio
`r sd_range("gaussian")`). For the Beta model they differ from INLA's by a
few percent (ratio `r sd_range("beta")`, smaller from $D = 1,000$ on), on the
CPU and on Metal alike. This difference comes from the method and the priors, which are
not identical in the two engines, and not from the device. The GPU evaluates
floating-point operations in a different order from the CPU, so the Metal and
CPU chains differ slightly, but they give the same estimates. The largest
split R-hat over all JAX fits is
`r sprintf("%.3f", max(rh$rhat_max, na.rm = TRUE))`.

## Using the Apple GPU

```r
# One-time setup of the Python environment with jax-metal
fastsae::setup_numpyro_env(device = "metal")

# In a new R session: request Metal before any other JAX fit
fit <- hb_area(y ~ x1 + x2, vardir = "vardir", data = df,
               engine = jax_engine(device = "metal"))
fit$device   # "metal:METAL:0"
```

jax-metal does not implement two operations used by NumPyro's NUTS sampler:
the bit count `popcnt`, and some `lax.cond` statements with constant outputs.
When `device = "metal"`, fastsae replaces both with equivalent operations
that Metal supports, and samples the chains sequentially. If a model still
cannot be compiled on Metal, the fit falls back to the CPU with a warning.

In short: for most surveys (hundreds to a few thousand domains),
`inla_engine()` is the fastest choice, and `jax_engine(device = "cpu")` is
the faster way to get full MCMC. `jax_engine(device = "metal")` becomes
worthwhile for very large numbers of domains.
